activities.anchor: inside sits a fluid loaded with potassium
activities.caption: file each ion — inside or outside
activities.name: apIonsBuckets

config.prompt: The membrane divides two seawater-and-salt fluids. File each player:
config.why: The sodium–potassium pump maintains the imbalance — 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, an ATP-burning exchange that is why the brain devours a fifth of your resting energy.

activities.anchor: The elegance is that no single step needs supervision
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the spike narrated
activities.name: apPhaseSpot

config.prompt: A student's phase-by-phase narration of the spike contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Inputs sum at the axon initial segment; past −55 mV the spike ignites.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open; the incoming positive charge depolarises the membrane further, opening more channels.
Sodium channels inactivate through a plug that swings shut independently of voltage; slower potassium channels let K⁺ rush out.
Potassium channels slam shut instantly at +40 mV, ending the spike before any overshoot.
The membrane overshoots rest into afterhyperpolarisation, then the pump and leak currents restore −70 mV.
config.correction: Potassium channels close gradually — the lingering efflux is what overshoots rest into afterhyperpolarisation, not an instant shutdown.
config.why: Each voltage opens the channel whose current creates the next voltage — a chain of feedbacks Hodgkin and Huxley captured in four coupled equations that predict, not describe.

activities.anchor: the spike does not consume or reverse the cell
activities.caption: true or false — the spike's energy bill
activities.name: apGradientJudge

statements.s: The ions crossing per spike are minuscule compared with the pool.
statements.why: A neuron can fire for a while on its stored gradients even with the pump poisoned.

statements.s: Each spike dramatically consumes or reverses the cell's ion gradients.
statements.why: The crossing per spike is minuscule — the drama is in the voltage change, not the chemistry spent.

statements.s: A neuron could fire spikes indefinitely with its pump poisoned.
statements.why: For a while, yes — but not indefinitely; the gradients run down.

statements.s: The ongoing metabolic bill is paid in restoring the gradients, not in firing them.
statements.why: The spike itself is passive channel chemistry; the pump does the slow bookkeeping.

activities.anchor: Rate rises roughly logarithmically with stimulus intensity
activities.caption: which curve matches frequency coding?
activities.name: apFreqTrace

config.prompt: A brighter light, a heavier weight, a louder tone. Which curve matches afferent firing rate against stimulus intensity?
config.why: Weber–Fechner territory: the spike never gets taller — the afferent fires faster, not harder, and precise spike timing carries extra information where circuits use it.

activities.anchor: The only way for a neuron to shout is faster, not louder
activities.caption: drag the divider — two stimuli, one spike
activities.name: apShoutCompare

config.prompt: The stimulus barely clears threshold, or doubles it. Drag the divider between the two cases:

before.label: Barely suprathreshold
before.text: The full, stereotyped spike — same amplitude, same shape. Subthreshold inputs, by contrast, produce nothing at all.

after.label: Stimulus doubled
after.text: The same spike again — intensity is encoded in how often spikes arrive, not how tall they are. There are no half-spikes and no shape variation to read meaning from.

config.why: The code is digital (uniform spikes) with its analogue content in the statistics: rate, rhythm, synchrony.

activities.anchor: conduction in thin naked axons runs at 0.5–2 m/s
activities.caption: rebuild the self-renewing wave
activities.name: apWaveOrder

config.prompt: A spike does not travel like a thrown ball — it re-erupts. Rebuild the sequence:
items: The depolarisation at the active patch spreads passively to the adjacent patch of membrane
That patch crosses threshold and its own sodium channels ignite
The spike regenerates at full amplitude — the signal never attenuates
In myelinated axons the regeneration happens only at the bare gaps — the nodes of Ranvier
Saltatory conduction: leaping node to node at up to 120 m/s
config.why: It arrives at the terminal exactly as tall as it left the trigger zone, whether the axon is a millimetre or a metre long — and myelin cuts the metabolic cost roughly tenfold for a given speed.

activities.anchor: That design constraint made myelin one of the decisive inventions
activities.caption: call the span — the longest axons afloat
activities.name: apWhaleEstimate

config.prompt: At the extreme of body size, how many metres long can a blue whale's motor axons to its hindquarters run?
config.why: Fifteen metres — without myelinated, 100-m/s-class conduction, an animal that size would be coordinating its hindquarters on multi-second delays.
config.context: A stretch reflex completes its metre-long round trip in tens of milliseconds; unmyelinated pain fibres ride the same distance a hundredfold slower.

activities.caption: pair each agent with its channel attack
activities.name: apToxinMatch

config.prompt: Evolution found the channels first; chemistry followed. Pair each agent with its attack:

pairs.right: binds the sodium channel's outer pore and blocks it — a few milligrams silence every spike
hold channels open or lock them shut
block the pore from inside, preferentially in open or inactivated states — use-dependent
exploit the same state-dependence to quiet runaway seizure firing

config.why: Each toxin's exquisite specificity made it a research tool — the dissection that produced the modern channel atlas, and 'channelopathy' as a disease category.
